children.text: Processes have a natural tendency to occur in one direction under a given set of conditions. Water naturally flows downhill, but uphill flow requires outside intervention, such as the use of a pump. Iron exposed to the earth’s atmosphere corrodes, but rust is not converted to iron without intentional chemical treatment. In thermodynamics, we call the direction that occurs naturally—that is, without needing an ongoing external force—a
A process that occurs naturally without the need for continuous input of energy from an external source.
. The opposite direction, then, constitutes a
A process that does not occur naturally and requires a continuous input of energy from an external source to proceed.
and will occur only if we drive it with an outside influence, such as a battery. The
All spontaneous processes result in an increase in the total entropy of the universe.
provides a powerful set of tools that allow us to determine the direction of spontaneity.

One consequence of the second law is that heat flows from objects with higher temperature to objects with lower temperature. Consider placing a hot metal rod into some cool water. The first law of thermodynamics is about conservation of energy: the amount of heat lost by the metal rod is equal to the amount of heat gained by the water. The second law is about the direction of the heat flow: the heat flows from the hot metal bar into the cool water. For this situation, the prediction of the second law seems obvious: the spontaneous direction is that for which the heat flows from hot to cold. But in this module, you will see how to make predictions that are not obvious using the second law of thermodynamics. In some cases, the spontaneous direction may even reverse as we change the conditions.

The spontaneity of a process is not correlated to the speed of the process. A spontaneous change may be so rapid that it is essentially instantaneous or so slow that it cannot be observed over any practical period of time. For example, consider the conversion of diamond into graphite:

of carbon at very high pressures, such as those present during its geologic formation, and graphite is the stable form under ambient atmospheric pressure. The conversion of diamond to graphite is thermodynamically spontaneous under typical ambient conditions, but diamonds continue to exist indefinitely at normal pressure and temperature because the conversion process is extremely slow. (For all practical purposes, diamonds are indeed “forever.”) Situations such as this emphasize the important distinction between the thermodynamic and the kinetic aspects of a process. children.text: The conversion of carbon from the diamond allotrope to the graphite allotrope is spontaneous at ambient pressure, but its rate is immeasurably slow at low to moderate temperatures. At high temperatures and pressures, the reverse process becomes both spontaneous and fast, providing a way to make industrial diamonds from graphite (Credit, diamond photo: Modification of work by "Fancy Diamonds"/Flickr. Credit, graphite photo: Modification of work by images-of-elements.com/carbon.php.)

The predictions of the second law depend on the conditions. For the conversion of graphite to diamond, under conditions of high temperature and high pressure, the spontaneous direction reverses and the conversion of graphite to diamond becomes spontaneous. For example, inexpensive industrial diamonds for drill bits and other applications can be made by converting graphite into diamond in an explosion that simultaneously pressurizes and heats up the graphite. (The resulting synthetic diamonds have too many defects and impurities to be used for jewelry.)

Keep in mind that the second law enables us to determine "what" can happen but not how long it will take to happen. Also remember that changing the conditions can alter the direction that is spontaneous.
